title: xAI × NVIDIA: Colossus 2 Compute Deal
summary: Negotiation on the Colossus 2 expansion. Agreed in principle on 350,000 Rubin-generation GPUs delivered in three tranches starting Q1 2027, with an option for 150,000 more gated on power availability; NVIDIA takes partial payment in compute credits for its own model work. Both agreed liquid-cooling rack specs must be locked jointly by September 15. They disagreed openly on chip export policy ahead of the Commerce briefing and agreed to keep that fight separate from the supply deal.
decisions: 350,000 Rubin GPUs in three tranches starting Q1 2027, option for 150,000 more gated on Colossus 2 power milestones
NVIDIA takes 8 percent of the deal value in Colossus compute credits
Joint engineering team locks the liquid-cooled rack and networking spec by September 15
Keep the export-policy disagreement separate from the supply relationship; both present at the Commerce briefing

action_items.task: Send the tranche delivery schedule with Rubin volume ramp assumptions and the compute-credit term sheet
Provide the Colossus 2 substation energization timeline and gigawatt phasing to size tranche two
Stand up the joint rack-spec engineering team with xAI infrastructure leads

transcript.speaker: Jensen Huang
transcript.text: Elon! Good to see you. I walked your Colossus 2 floor an hour ago — I have to say it, nobody stands up capacity like your team. Nobody. The first Colossus in 122 days broke everyone's brains at my company. We still use it in slides.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: And I still use your margins in mine. Good to see you, Jensen. Let's do the fun part — I need a lot of chips, you have all the chips, and we're going to argue about export policy at some point, so let's do commerce before combat.

transcript.speaker: Jensen Huang
transcript.text: Ha! Commerce before combat, I'm stealing that. Okay. Tell me the shape of it. What does Grok 5 need?

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Grok 5 trains on what we have. This buy is Grok 6 and the video-world-model line. The shape is: half a million Rubin-class GPUs landing across 2027, coherent, one fabric, one building. Colossus 2 is being built for 1.5 gigawatts. I want to be your biggest single-site deployment on Earth, and I want the pricing to reflect that I'm the easiest large customer you have — one site, one contract, no committee.

transcript.speaker: Jensen Huang
transcript.text: You are the easiest and also the most demanding, which is the best kind of customer. Here's my honesty in return: half a million Rubin in calendar 2027 from one customer is more than I can commit today. CoWoS packaging is the gate, it's always packaging. What I can commit is 350,000 across three tranches starting Q1, and an option on the next 150,000 that we both size in mid-2027 when I see my supply and you see your power.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: The option gated on what, exactly? Because if it's gated on your supply I'm just last in line with extra steps.

transcript.speaker: Jensen Huang
transcript.text: Gated on your power, actually. Elon, I've watched three customers this year take delivery of GPUs that sat in crates because their substations weren't energized. It's heartbreaking, it's like — you buy a Ferrari and you have no road. Show me Colossus 2 hitting its gigawatt phasing milestones and the option converts automatically at tranche pricing. Your electricians control the gate, not my sales team.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: That's actually fair, and slightly annoying, because power is genuinely my long pole. The substation timeline says 800 megawatts energized by March, 1.5 gigawatts by October 2027. I'll send you the phasing with the tranche sizes mapped to it. If the White House fast-track pilot happens — the interconnect thing I've been pushing — those dates improve by a quarter.

transcript.speaker: Jensen Huang
transcript.text: I saw the fast-track reporting. For once you and I are lobbying the same direction — anything that gets American data centers powered faster sells more of my chips and trains more of your models. Okay, pricing. Volume like this, you know I take care of you, but I want something too. I want compute back.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Explain.

transcript.speaker: Jensen Huang
transcript.text: NVIDIA trains models now — foundation models for robotics, for chip design, our own research. We're always short of large coherent clusters because we sell them all, it's a ridiculous problem, the shoemaker's children have no shoes. So: 8 percent of the deal value comes back to me as Colossus compute credits. I get burst capacity on the biggest coherent cluster in the world, you get effectively a discount that doesn't show up as a discount, which we both know your CFO and my CFO will each claim as a win.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Hilarious and accepted, with one carve-out: your workloads run in a partition with no access to Grok training data or checkpoints, our security team owns the isolation design, and your robotics models don't get trained on anything derived from Tesla fleet data even by accident. You're a supplier and also a competitor to Optimus, we're both adults about it.

transcript.speaker: Jensen Huang
transcript.text: Both adults about it — agreed, hard isolation, your team specs it, my team lives with it. Honestly I'd insist on the same in your position. Okay, engineering. Rubin racks at your density are liquid-cooled at specs nobody's deployed at site scale. Last time, your team modified our reference design in the field and it was — I'll say it diplomatically — better in two ways and terrifying in one.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: The terrifying way worked fine.

transcript.speaker: Jensen Huang
transcript.text: It worked fine at 100,000 GPUs! At 350,000 the coolant manifold tolerances that terrified my engineers become a statistics problem, and statistics always wins. Proposal: joint engineering team, your infrastructure leads and my GB-systems people, lock the rack and networking spec together by September 15 so tranche one ships as a known quantity. No field surprises, in either direction.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Agreed — joint team, spec locked September 15. Put your best networking person on it; the fabric is where I actually worry. At this scale the all-reduce is the computer. If the fabric stalls, I own half a million space heaters.

transcript.speaker: Jensen Huang
transcript.text: The most expensive space heaters in history. You'll have my best. Okay — commerce concluded, and it's a beautiful deal, genuinely, this is the biggest single-site commitment we've ever signed. Now. Combat. The Commerce briefing on the 11th. You've been telling the White House to keep my frontier chips locked up.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: I've been telling them to restrict the frontier tier for two years and sell everything else freely. Jensen, capability tracks compute. You know this better than anyone alive, you built the curve. Every top-tier chip exported in volume is a direct transfer of frontier capability, and unlike cars or phones, this particular product is the lead in the most important race in history.

transcript.speaker: Jensen Huang
transcript.text: And I think that mental model is two years stale. The restriction doesn't freeze anyone — it accelerates them. We restricted, and what happened? Their domestic chips got better faster, their whole stack decoupled from ours, and American companies lost the revenue that funds the next generation. You don't stay ahead by hiding the product, you stay ahead by running faster, and running faster costs money, which is revenue, which is exports. I'd rather the world build on my architecture than learn to live without it.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: The ecosystem argument is your strongest one and it's still not worth the frontier tier. Sell them the N-minus-one generation — they build on your architecture, you keep the revenue, and the actual frontier stays here for twenty-four months. That's my whole position. It costs you, what, single-digit percent of revenue? For a real lead in the thing that matters most?

transcript.speaker: Jensen Huang
transcript.text: It costs more than single digits and the lead it buys is smaller than you think — but look, this is why the briefing exists. You bring your capability projections, I bring my ecosystem data, and Commerce earns their salaries for once. What I want from you today is just this: whatever they decide, it doesn't touch this table. The supply deal, the joint team, the credits — separate from the fight.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Agreed and easy — I've disagreed with you about something publicly for approximately every year I've known you and I've bought chips from you every one of those years. The deal is the deal. And at the briefing I'll say NVIDIA's the best in the world at what it does right before I argue for restricting it, which will be very funny.

transcript.speaker: Jensen Huang
transcript.text: I'll say Elon's projections are brilliant right before I explain why they're wrong. We should sell tickets. Okay: my team sends the tranche schedule and credit term sheet by the 17th, you send power phasing by the 20th, joint team stood up by the 24th, spec locked September 15. And Elon — when Grok 6 trains on this thing, I want to see the loss curves. Professional curiosity.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: You'll see the loss curves when your compute credits earn you a seat in the war room, which — I just realized — is exactly what you negotiated. Well played. Alright, done. Biggest cluster in history. Try to make enough chips this time.
